rows.tag: INR the day after parenteral vitamin K

items.label: Sepsis or shock, low platelets or fibrinogen

tiers.text: INR ≥ 2.0 not corrected by vitamin K meets the PALF coagulopathy criterion (with acute liver injury; in known chronic liver disease it is decompensation). Call hepatology and the transplant center now; PICU. If bleeding: IV vitamin K; PCC or plasma for life-threatening bleeding; head imaging in an infant.

Encephalopathy or hypoglycemia with a prolonged INR: treat as acute liver failure. With encephalopathy, an INR ≥ 1.5 after vitamin K meets the PALF criterion. Call hepatology and the transplant center now; PICU. If bleeding: IV vitamin K; PCC or plasma for life-threatening bleeding; head imaging in an infant.
Active bleeding: emergency department / PICU now. IV vitamin K; head imaging in an infant; check platelets and fibrinogen. PCC or plasma for life-threatening bleeding, not for the number.
Think consumption (DIC): factors V and VIII both low, fibrinogen falling. Treat sepsis or shock; PICU.
Not corrected by vitamin K. Send factors V, VII, VIII and fibrinogen; check mental status and glucose; call hepatology today. If encephalopathy appears, this is PALF — call the transplant center.

Still prolonged: deficiency may sit on top of liver disease. Factor V decides — low factor V means the hepatocytes are failing. Call hepatology today. In an infant: fractionated bilirubin and stool color today.
Infant: vitamin K deficiency can be the first sign of biliary atresia. Fractionated bilirubin and stool color today; call hepatology.

Vitamin K deficiency, not synthetic failure. Find the cause: cholestasis (direct bilirubin, GGT, stool color), malabsorption, antibiotics, poor intake. In cholestasis continue daily vitamin K and check INR every visit.

rule.noneText: Give parenteral vitamin K (IV or subcutaneous, not oral), recheck the INR the next day, then pick the result.
